questions.question: What is a Bounded Context in Domain-Driven Design and why does it matter?
questions.title: Bounded Context — What It Is and Why It Matters
questions.direct_answer: A **Bounded Context** is an explicit boundary within which a particular domain model has **one consistent meaning**. The same word — 'Customer', 'Order', 'Product' — can mean entirely different things in different contexts: in **Sales** a Customer is a prospect with a lead score, in **Shipping** it's a delivery address, in **Support** it's a ticket holder. Bounded Contexts prevent the corruption of a single 'one-size-fits-all' model by keeping each model focused, internally consistent, and translated explicitly at boundaries. **A Bounded Context is a design boundary, not a deployment unit** — a monolith can host many BCs as modules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Why a single unified model fails at organizational scale, the role of Ubiquitous Language inside each context, and the distinction between BC (design) and microservice (deployment).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Equating 'Bounded Context = microservice', or trying to build one canonical model that 'covers' the whole enterprise.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Context Maps and integration patterns (Customer/Supplier, Conformist, Anti-Corruption Layer, Shared Kernel), enforcement via ArchUnit / Java modules, and how data ownership per BC enables clean later extraction.

sections.title: The Unified-Model Trap
sections.content:
In any non-trivial enterprise, different teams use the same business words to mean fundamentally different things.

- **Sales** says 'Customer' → a prospect with a lead score, an assigned rep, an opportunity pipeline.
- **Shipping** says 'Customer' → a delivery address with packaging preferences and a signature requirement.
- **Support** says 'Customer' → a ticket holder with an SLA tier and contact preferences.

The natural instinct is to build **one** `Customer` class that serves everyone. This is exactly how domain models become incoherent:

- The class accumulates fields nobody in any single team needs.
- Adding a sales-specific field touches code that ships with shipping deploys.
- Validation rules contradict each other (Sales allows incomplete addresses; Shipping requires them).
- The class's responsibilities mirror the org chart, not a coherent concept.

**Bounded Contexts** solve this by drawing **explicit boundaries** around cohesive models, where every term has **one precise meaning** — the **Ubiquitous Language** of that context. The duplication across contexts is intentional: it's far cheaper than the coupling a unified model creates.

Three different `Customer` classes. **All correct.** - Cross-context flow happens through **events with primitive payloads**, not by importing each other's domain classes. - Each context is its own world internally; the boundary is the only place translation happens.

sections.title: Ubiquitous Language Per Context
BC ≠ Microservice (The Most Common Confusion)
sections.content:
A Bounded Context is a **design boundary**. A microservice is a **deployment unit**. They are related but not the same.

- A monolith can contain **many** Bounded Contexts as separate top-level packages or Java modules.
- A microservice **typically** corresponds to one BC — but a single BC can be backed by multiple physical services (one for command-side, one for query-side under CQRS).
- You decide BC boundaries **first** (by language, by team, by data ownership). You decide deployment **second**.

**Why this matters:** equating them leads to **premature decomposition** — splitting into microservices before you understand the domain, drawing service boundaries on the wrong lines, and then living with the cross-service refactor pain.

**Modular monolith** is often the right starting point: BCs as modules, sharing a deployable, ready to extract when team / scaling pressure justifies it.

sections.title: Enforcing Boundaries in Code
sections.content:
Without enforcement, the boundary erodes silently — a developer 'just imports' another context's domain class because 'it already has the field I need.'

**Java packaging:**
```
com.company/
  sales/
    domain/, application/, adapter/
  shipping/
    domain/, application/, adapter/
  support/
    domain/, application/, adapter/
  shared/
    Money.java, EmailAddress.java         // shared kernel: very small, very stable
```

**ArchUnit enforcement at build time:**
```java
@ArchTest
static final ArchRule salesDoesNotDependOnShipping =
    noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..sales..")
        .should().dependOnClassesThat()
        .resideInAPackage("..shipping..");

@ArchTest
static final ArchRule onlySharedKernelIsCrossContext =
    classes().that().resideInAnyPackage("..sales.domain..", "..shipping.domain..")
        .should().onlyDependOnClassesThat()
        .resideInAnyPackage("..sales.domain..", "..shipping.domain..", "..shared..", "java..");
```

**Java 9+ modules** (`module-info.java`) give compile-time enforcement — internal classes of one BC are simply invisible to another.

sections.title: Data Ownership Per Context
sections.content:
Each BC owns its **own tables / schema**, even within a shared database instance:

- `sales.customers` (lead_score, rep_id, opportunity_count, ...)
- `shipping.customers` (default_address_id, packaging_preference, ...)
- `support.customers` (sla_tier, last_contact_at, open_ticket_count, ...)

**No cross-context joins.** When Shipping needs the customer's name from Sales, the name is delivered as part of an **event payload** (`OrderSubmittedEvent { customerId, customerName, ... }`) and **stored locally** in `shipping.customers` — a denormalized copy.

**Why this matters:**

- Each BC functions even if the others are temporarily unavailable.
- Schema migrations don't cascade; Sales can rename a column without breaking Shipping.
- Future microservice extraction = replace in-process events with Kafka, move schema to its own DB. The domain model and application logic don't change.

Teams that skip data isolation in the monolith phase discover that microservice extraction requires a painful, risky data migration that could have been avoided.

sections.title: Translation at Boundaries
sections.content:
When data must cross a context boundary, **never share domain classes**. Use one of: - **Domain events** with primitive payloads (`OrderSubmittedEvent { customerId: String, totalCents: long, currency: String }`). - **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)** — an adapter in the consuming context that translates the foreign model into the local model. Critical when integrating with legacy or third-party systems. - **Published Language** — an explicitly maintained, versioned schema (Avro, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that both contexts agree on. - **Shared Kernel** — a tiny set of common value objects (`Money`, `EmailAddress`, `CustomerId`) that both contexts depend on. Keep it **small and stable**; large shared kernels reintroduce coupling. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Sales Customer
internal model] --> Trans[ACL / Mapper] Trans --> B[Shipping Customer
internal model] ``` **Rule:** the consuming context controls the translation. Never let a 'Customer DTO from Sales' leak into Shipping's domain layer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'BC = microservice.'** Conflates design and deployment. Many BCs in a monolith is a perfectly valid (and often better) starting point.
- **One canonical model.** A `Customer` god-class in a `common` package that all teams import — the textbook anti-pattern this is meant to fix.
- **Cross-context table joins.** SQL `JOIN sales_customer s ON s.id = shipping_customer.id` defeats data isolation; one slow query degrades both contexts.
- **Sharing domain classes via a `common` library.** A 'common-domain' Maven module that grows organically is a unified model with extra steps.
- **No build-time enforcement.** Without ArchUnit / Java modules, boundaries erode in PRs nobody flags.
- **Skipping the language conversation.** Boundaries follow language; if you draw boundaries on technical lines (e.g. 'one BC for read, one for write'), you've drawn them wrong.
- **Over-fragmenting.** Two BCs for what is genuinely one model just adds translation overhead. Boundaries should be discovered, not invented.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **A Bounded Context is an explicit boundary** within which one model, one Ubiquitous Language, one consistent meaning of every term applies.
- **Same word, different meaning** — `Customer` in Sales ≠ `Customer` in Shipping; the duplication is intentional.
- **BC is a design boundary, not a microservice** — a monolith can contain many BCs as modules.
- **Each BC owns its data** (own schema/tables); cross-context flow happens via events or APIs.
- **Translation at boundaries** via ACL, domain events, Published Language, or a small Shared Kernel.
- **Enforce in code** with ArchUnit rules or Java modules.
- **Discovered, not invented** — follow the language; boundaries emerge from how the business actually thinks.
- **Microservice extraction is a deployment decision**; if you've kept BCs clean, the extraction is mechanical.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The unified-model trap**

In any non-trivial enterprise, different teams use the same words to mean different things. Sales 'Customer' is a prospect with a lead score. Shipping 'Customer' is a delivery address. Support 'Customer' is a ticket holder.

The instinct is to build one Customer class that serves everyone — and that's exactly how domain models become incoherent. The class accumulates fields nobody needs, validation rules contradict each other, and a sales-specific change ships with shipping deploys.

Bounded Contexts solve this by drawing explicit boundaries around cohesive models, each with its own Ubiquitous Language, where every term has one precise meaning. The duplication across contexts is intentional — it's cheaper than the coupling a unified model creates.

**Visualizing the boundary**

Three contexts, three different Customer classes, all correct. Cross-context flow happens through events with primitive payloads (OrderSubmittedEvent), not by importing each other's domain classes.

**Ubiquitous Language per context**

A BC has its own vocabulary that lives in the code. Sales: customer.qualify(criteria), Opportunity. Support: customer.escalate(reason), Ticket. The verbs and nouns are different because the language is different.

If you and a domain expert disagree about what a word means, ask which context they're in. If the answer is 'both' — you've found a boundary.

**BC ≠ microservice**

Most common confusion. A BC is a design boundary; a microservice is a deployment unit.

- A monolith can contain many BCs as separate top-level packages or Java modules
- A microservice typically corresponds to one BC — but a single BC can be backed by multiple physical services (CQRS read + write)
- Decide BC boundaries first (language, team, data); deployment second

Equating them leads to premature decomposition — splitting before you understand the domain, drawing boundaries on the wrong lines.

Modular monolith is often the right start: BCs as modules, sharing a deployable, ready to extract when team/scaling pressure justifies.

**Enforcing boundaries in code**

Without enforcement, boundaries erode — 'just import Customer from sales because it has the field I need.'

Java packaging: com.company.sales.*, com.company.shipping.*, com.company.shared (tiny stable kernel).

ArchUnit rules in CI: noClasses().that().resideInAPackage('..sales..').should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage('..shipping..'). Build fails on violation.

Java 9+ modules give compile-time enforcement — internal classes invisible cross-BC.

**Data ownership per context**

Each BC owns its own tables/schema, even in a shared DB. sales.customers, shipping.customers, support.customers — separate.

No cross-context joins. Shipping needs customer name from Sales? It arrives in OrderSubmittedEvent payload and stored locally in shipping.customers — denormalized copy.

Why: each BC functions if others unavailable. Schema migrations don't cascade. Future microservice extraction = replace in-process events with Kafka, move schema to its own DB. Domain model and app logic don't change.

Skipping data isolation in monolith phase → painful microservice extraction later.

**Translation at boundaries**

Never share domain classes. Use:

- Domain events with primitive payloads
- Anti-Corruption Layer in consuming context (translates foreign model to local). Critical for legacy/third-party integration
- Published Language — versioned schema (Avro, Protobuf, OpenAPI) both sides agree on
- Shared Kernel — small set of common value objects (Money, EmailAddress, CustomerId). Keep small and stable

Rule: the consuming context controls the translation.

**Common mistakes**

- 'BC = microservice'
- One canonical Customer class in a common package
- Cross-context table joins
- 'common-domain' Maven module that grows organically — unified model with extra steps
- No build-time enforcement
- Boundaries on technical lines (read vs write) instead of language lines
- Over-fragmenting — two BCs for what is genuinely one model

**Recommendation**

**Discover Bounded Contexts by language and team boundaries, not by technical or deployment concerns. Implement them as packages or Java modules in a monolith first; let microservice extraction be a separate, deferred decision. Each BC owns its data, expresses its own Ubiquitous Language in code, and translates explicitly at boundaries via events, an ACL, or a small Shared Kernel. Enforce the boundary with ArchUnit in CI. Equating BC with microservice is the single most common DDD mistake — it leads to premature decomposition and cross-service refactor pain.**

questions.question: What is the difference between an Entity and a Value Object in DDD?
questions.title: Entity vs Value Object in DDD
questions.direct_answer: An **Entity** has a **unique identity that persists through state changes** — two `Order`s with the same items are not the same Order if they have different IDs. A **Value Object** has **no identity** — it's defined entirely by its attributes; two `Money(50, USD)` instances are completely interchangeable. **Entities are mutable** through controlled domain methods; **Value Objects are immutable** and replaced wholesale. The distinction drives equality, mutability, JPA mapping (`@Entity` vs `@Embeddable`), and whether the concept gets its own database table.

interviewer_intent.testing: When identity matters vs when attribute equality is enough; how this distinction reshapes equality, mutability, and persistence.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Slapping `@Entity` and a `Long id` on every class — making `Money`, `Address`, and `DateRange` into entities with surrogate keys for no domain reason.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show concrete value-object benefits (thread safety, no aliasing bugs, behavior on the type), records as VO implementation, and the JPA mapping consequences.

sections.title: Why the Distinction Matters
sections.content:
Most developers default to `Long id` and `@Entity` on every class in their domain. The result:

- `Money` has a primary key. `Address` has a primary key. `DateRange` has a primary key.
- None of those keys represent any real-world identity.
- Unnecessary tables, pointless joins, ORM-shaped models.
- Aliasing bugs ("why did changing this address change my customer's billing address too?").

DDD's Entity vs Value Object distinction prevents this:

- **Entity:** something that has continuity through time and identity that matters. Your bank account stays 'your account' even after deposits and withdrawals change its balance. The account number matters; the balance is just current state.
- **Value Object:** a measurement, description, or quantity. A price, an address, a date range, a coordinate. Two instances with the same attributes are completely interchangeable — there's no distinction between 'this fifty dollars' and 'that fifty dollars'.

Getting this right cascades into equality, mutability, persistence, and threading. Getting it wrong produces phantom identity and a leaky persistence model.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Entity | Value Object |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Unique ID; identity persists through state changes | None; defined entirely by attributes |
| Equality | By ID (`order1.id.equals(order2.id)`) | By all attributes (same amount + currency = same `Money`) |
| Mutability | Mutable via controlled domain methods | Immutable — replaced wholesale, never modified in place |
| Java idiom | Class with private state and behavior; identity field | `record` or final class; no setters |
| JPA mapping | `@Entity` with `@Id` — owns its own table | `@Embeddable` — columns live inside the owning entity's row |
| Thread safety | Requires synchronization if shared across threads | Inherently thread-safe |
| Sharing | Aliasing risk if shared without care | Safe to share freely |
| Lifecycle | Independent — persists in its own right | Dependent — lives within an entity |
| Examples | `Order`, `Customer`, `Account`, `Shipment` | `Money`, `Address`, `DateRange`, `EmailAddress`, `Coordinates` |

sections.title: Value Objects in Java — Records and Behavior
Entities in Java — Identity and Controlled State
JPA Mapping — `@Entity` vs `@Embeddable`
How to Decide — The Identity Test
sections.content:
Ask: **'If I change one of its attributes, is it still the same thing?'**

- **Yes → Entity.** Your bank account with a different balance is still your account. Same `Order` after status changes from PENDING to CONFIRMED.
- **No → Value Object.** A different amount of money is a *different* money. A different street is a *different* address. A different date is a *different* date.

Another test: **'Are two of them with identical attributes interchangeable?'**

- **Yes → Value Object.** $50 is $50; you don't care which $50.
- **No → Entity.** Your savings account with $50 is *not* your friend's savings account with $50.

**Borderline cases:**
- An `Address` is usually a VO. But for a real estate app where 'this house' has identity tied to the address, the Property is an entity that contains an Address VO.
- A `Person` is almost always an entity — even identical twins are different people.
- A `Color` is usually a VO unless you're a paint company managing color SKUs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@Entity` on everything.** Address, Money, DateRange as entities with surrogate keys — phantom identity, unnecessary tables, joins everywhere.
- **Mutable value objects.** Setters on `Money` lead to aliasing bugs (`order1.total = order2.total; order1.total.setAmount(...)` mutates both).
- **Equality by reference for VOs.** Forgetting to override `equals`/`hashCode` (or using records) so two `Money(50, USD)` are unequal in a `Set`.
- **Equality by attributes for entities.** Two `Customer`s with the same name and email aren't necessarily the same customer.
- **Long primitive IDs everywhere.** A method signature `transfer(Long, Long, Long)` is unreadable; strongly typed `OrderId`, `AccountId`, `Money` value objects make APIs self-documenting.
- **Putting business logic in services rather than VOs.** `MoneyUtils.add(a, b)` instead of `a.plus(b)`; the behavior belongs on the type.
- **Shared mutable state through entities.** Returning `order.getItems()` directly lets callers mutate internal state; return `List.copyOf(items)` or use immutable collections.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Entity:** identity that persists through state changes; equals by ID; mutable through controlled methods; `@Entity`.
- **Value Object:** no identity; equals by attributes; immutable; `@Embeddable` (no own table).
- **Records** are perfect VO implementations in modern Java.
- **Behavior on the type** — `money.plus(other)`, not a service.
- **Strongly typed IDs** (`OrderId` as a VO) make APIs self-documenting and catch wrong-type bugs at compile time.
- **Identity test:** if changing an attribute makes it a different thing, it's a VO.
- **Wrong default:** making everything an entity for ORM convenience.
- **VO benefits:** thread safety, no aliasing, validation at construction, behavior co-located with data.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Why the distinction matters**

Most developers default to Long id + @Entity on everything. Money, Address, DateRange all become entities with surrogate keys for no domain reason — unnecessary tables, pointless joins, aliasing bugs.

DDD's distinction:

- Entity: continuity through time, identity matters. Bank account stays 'your account' through deposits/withdrawals
- Value Object: a measurement, description, quantity. A price, address, date range. Two with same attributes are completely interchangeable — 'this $50' = 'that $50'

Getting it right cascades into equality, mutability, persistence, threading.

**Side by side**

Identity: ID vs none.
Equality: by ID vs by attributes.
Mutability: controlled mutation vs immutable, replaced wholesale.
Java: class with private state vs record / final class.
JPA: @Entity (own table) vs @Embeddable (columns in owning row).
Thread safety: needs sync vs inherently safe.
Lifecycle: independent vs lives within entity.
Examples: Order, Customer, Account vs Money, Address, DateRange, EmailAddress.

**Value Objects in Java — records + behavior**

Money as record(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency). Compact constructor validates invariants. plus() returns new Money; throws if currency mismatched — invalid arithmetic impossible by design. times(qty), isGreaterThan(other) — behavior on the type.

Records auto-generate equals/hashCode/toString based on components. Attribute-based equality automatic. No setters — every operation returns new Money.

**Entities — identity and controlled state**

Order with OrderId identity, CustomerId, items, status, total. Constructor validates 'order needs items'. cancel() is a named business method, throws if shipped. Equals based on id only. State changes only through named methods, never raw setters.

OrderId itself is a value object — strongly typed, can't pass CustomerId where OrderId expected.

**JPA mapping**

Order is @Entity with @Id, owns its row. Money is @Embeddable; its columns live inside the order's row (total_amount, total_currency). No separate table, no join.

Wrong: @Entity Money with @GeneratedValue Long id. Now every order has FK to money table; every line item creates two extra rows; queries explode in joins. None represents real domain identity.

**The identity test**

'If I change one of its attributes, is it still the same thing?'

- Yes → Entity. Bank account with different balance is still your account
- No → VO. Different amount of money is different money. Different street is different address

Another test: 'Are two of them with identical attributes interchangeable?' Yes = VO; No = Entity.

Borderline: Address usually VO. For real estate, Property is entity containing Address VO. Person almost always entity. Color usually VO unless paint company managing SKUs.

**Common mistakes**

- @Entity on everything — phantom identity, unnecessary tables
- Mutable value objects — aliasing bugs
- Equality by reference for VOs — forgetting to override equals/hashCode
- Equality by attributes for entities — two Customers with same name aren't the same
- Long primitive IDs everywhere — transfer(Long, Long, Long) unreadable; strongly typed VOs make APIs self-documenting
- Service-style behavior — MoneyUtils.add(a, b) instead of a.plus(b)
- Returning mutable collections from entities — callers mutate internal state

**Recommendation**

**Default to Value Objects for measurements, descriptions, quantities, and IDs — use Java records with validation in compact constructors and behavior as methods on the type. Use Entities only when identity persists through state changes (Order, Customer, Account). Map VOs as @Embeddable in JPA — columns inside the owning entity's row, not separate tables. Strongly typed IDs (OrderId, CustomerId) as VOs prevent whole categories of bugs at compile time. The identity test ('still the same thing if attributes change?') is the deciding factor.**

questions.question: What is an Aggregate and Aggregate Root in DDD, and what are the design rules?
questions.title: Aggregate and Aggregate Root in DDD
questions.direct_answer: An **Aggregate** is a **cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency boundary** — the unit of transactional change. The **Aggregate Root** is the one entity inside the aggregate that **external code is allowed to reference**; all access to inner objects goes through the root, which enforces invariants. **Rules:** (1) one transaction modifies one aggregate; (2) reference other aggregates by ID, not by object reference; (3) keep aggregates small for concurrency; (4) all invariants that must hold transactionally live inside one aggregate. This is what makes DDD's tactical patterns scale and stay consistent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Aggregate as a consistency boundary, the root as the only allowed reference, the four design rules, and how aggregate size affects performance / concurrency.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Modeling huge aggregates ('Customer with all their orders, addresses, payments') that lock the world on every change, or referencing other aggregates by object instead of by ID.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss optimistic concurrency, eventual consistency between aggregates, and how aggregate boundaries map to repositories and microservices.

sections.title: The Problem Aggregates Solve
sections.content:
Domain models without explicit consistency boundaries develop two kinds of pathology:

1. **Inconsistent state.** Two requests both read an order, both add a line item, both save — one update overwrites the other. The order's `total` doesn't match its items.
2. **Lock contention.** A 'Customer' object that contains all of the customer's orders, addresses, and payment methods becomes a contention hotspot — every order-placement locks the entire customer.

Aggregates address both:

- An **aggregate** is a small cluster of objects (entities + value objects) that **change together**.
- The **aggregate root** is the entrance to the aggregate — external code holds a reference only to the root.
- One transaction modifies one aggregate. Multi-aggregate consistency is **eventual**, not transactional.
- Invariants that span the aggregate (e.g., 'order total = sum of items') are enforced inside the root.

**Result:** small consistency boundaries, predictable concurrency, no aliasing of internal state.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The problem aggregates solve**

Domain models without explicit consistency boundaries develop two pathologies:

1. Inconsistent state — two requests both read an order, both add a line, both save; one overwrites; total no longer matches items
2. Lock contention — a Customer god-object containing all orders/addresses/payments becomes contention hotspot; every order-placement locks the whole customer

Aggregates fix both:

- Aggregate is a small cluster (entities + value objects) that change together
- Aggregate root is the entrance — external code holds reference only to the root
- One transaction modifies one aggregate; multi-aggregate consistency is eventual
- Invariants spanning the aggregate enforced inside the root

**Anatomy**

Order aggregate: Order (root), OrderItems, ShippingInfo, PaymentMethod (VO). External code only allowed to touch Order. Internal entities reachable only through root. References to other aggregates (Customer, Product) by ID, not by object.

**Code example**

Order class with OrderId, CustomerId (by ID), List<OrderItem>, status, total, version. Constructor validates 'order needs items'. addItem(productId, qty, unitPrice) checks status, adds item, recomputes total — invariant 'total = sum of items' structurally impossible to violate. items() returns List.copyOf(items) — callers can't mutate internal list.

OrderItem created only through Order.addItem(); no external new OrderItem reachable.

**The four rules**

Rule 1: Reference other aggregates by ID, not object. private CustomerId, not private Customer. Object reference triggers lazy load, hidden joins, hidden contention.

Rule 2: One transaction, one aggregate. Multi-aggregate updates across transactions, coordinated via domain events and eventual consistency. Don't change customer.recordOrder(order) and orderRepo.save(order) in same transaction — publish OrderPlacedEvent; customer updates in a separate transaction.

Rule 3: Aggregates should be small. Customer with 5000 orders inside = contention, heavy loads, memory pressure. If thousands of internal entities, too big.

Rule 4: All invariants that must hold transactionally live inside one aggregate. 'Order total = sum of items' must always be true → items inside order aggregate. 'Customer max 3 active orders' → either model inside customer or relax to eventually consistent (preferable).

**Optimistic locking on the root**

@Version on root. JPA increments version on UPDATE, adds WHERE version = ?. Concurrent updates: second sees 0 rows updated → OptimisticLockException. Use case retries or returns 409 Conflict.

Works at aggregate level: root carries version; updating any internal entity bumps root's version. Concurrency detected at consistency-boundary level, not per-row — matches design intent.

**Aggregates and repositories**

One repository per aggregate. Deals with root only. OrderRepository.save(order), findById(orderId), findActiveByCustomerId(customerId).

Anti-pattern: OrderRepository + OrderItemRepository + ShippingInfoRepository. Fragments the aggregate, leaks persistence model upward, makes use case orchestrate four saves for one logical change.

Right: orderRepo.save(order) persists root + internal entities atomically. Persistence adapter handles multi-table mapping internally.

**Cross-aggregate consistency — domain events**

Order.submit() raises OrderSubmittedEvent. Use case publishes events after persistence. Other aggregate consumes in its own transaction (Customer.recordOrder).

Eventually consistent. Brief window where Order submitted but Customer hasn't recorded. For reliable delivery: transactional outbox — events written to outbox table in same transaction; background process publishes from outbox to Kafka.

**Common mistakes**

- Object references to other aggregates — hidden joins/lazy loads/contention
- Multiple aggregates in one transaction — breaks boundary
- Huge aggregates — contention and load explode
- Externally constructing internal entities — breaks invariant enforcement
- No optimistic lock — last-write-wins corruption
- Returning mutable internal collections — callers bypass Order.addItem; use defensive copies
- Repository per JPA entity — fragments aggregate
- Trying to enforce all invariants transactionally — some are inherently cross-aggregate (uniqueness across all customers); model as eventual

**Recommendation**

**Design aggregates as small consistency boundaries: the root is the only external entry point, internal entities are reachable only through the root, references to other aggregates are by ID, and one transaction modifies one aggregate. Use optimistic locking (@Version) on the root, one repository per aggregate that persists root and internals atomically, and domain events plus transactional outbox for cross-aggregate consistency. Keep aggregates small — if you find yourself loading thousands of internal entities or contending on a single root, the aggregate is too big and needs splitting.**

questions.question: What are Domain Events in DDD and how do you implement them in Java?
questions.title: Domain Events in DDD — Java Implementation
questions.direct_answer: A **Domain Event** is a **named, past-tense business fact** that something important happened in the domain (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentCaptured`, `UserRegistered`). Aggregates **raise** events when state changes; the application layer **publishes** them after persistence; other parts of the system **subscribe** to react. Events make cross-aggregate consistency, integration, and audit possible without coupling components. **In Java + Spring**, raise events inside aggregate methods, drain them after save, publish via `ApplicationEventPublisher` or a transactional outbox for reliable cross-service delivery.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Publishing events inside a transaction (consumer sees event before DB committed), or modeling 'events' as CRUD diffs (`CustomerUpdated{name, email}`).

sections.title: What a Domain Event Is
sections.content:
A domain event is a **fact**: something happened that the business cares about, named in **past tense**, **immutable** once raised, **describing what occurred** rather than commanding what should happen.

**Good event names:**
- `OrderPlaced`
- `PaymentCaptured`
- `EmailVerified`
- `InventoryReserved`
- `RefundIssued`

**Bad event names** (commands or CRUD diffs):
- `PlaceOrder` (a command, not a fact)
- `CustomerUpdated` (CRUD diff — says nothing about what business event happened)
- `RowChanged` (technical, not domain)

Good events make the system **expressive, integratable, and auditable**:
- Multiple subscribers can react without the producer knowing.
- The event log becomes the audit log for free.
- Eventual consistency between aggregates and services is natural.

polls outbox] Worker --> Kafka[(Kafka)] Kafka --> Other[Other services] ``` In one transaction: 1. Save the aggregate. 2. Insert event rows into an `outbox` table. A separate worker polls the outbox, publishes to Kafka, marks rows as published. If Kafka is down, the worker retries; the outbox guarantees no event is lost. ```sql CREATE TABLE outbox ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, aggregate_id VARCHAR(64), event_type VARCHAR(64), payload JSONB, occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ, published_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL ); ``` ```java @Transactional public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) { Order o = Order.create(cmd.customerId(), cmd.items()); orderRepo.save(o); for (DomainEvent e : o.drainEvents()) { outboxRepo.save(OutboxEntry.from(e)); // same transaction } return o; } ``` **Modern alternatives:** - **CDC (Debezium)** streams the outbox table directly to Kafka — no separate worker. - **Kafka transactions** can also achieve this, but outbox is simpler and more portable.

sections.title: Idempotent Consumers — At-Least-Once Reality
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Commands disguised as events.** `PlaceOrder` published 'as an event' is a command — it's telling the system to do something, not stating a fact.
- **CRUD events.** `CustomerUpdated{name, email, address}` says what changed but not why; subscribers can't reconstruct business meaning.
- **Publishing inside the transaction.** Consumer reads stale data or sees phantom events on rollback.
- **Including entire aggregates in events.** Events bloat; coupling to producer schema; serialization overhead.
- **Dual writes.** Save DB + publish Kafka outside an outbox — inevitable inconsistency.
- **Non-idempotent consumers.** Duplicate event → duplicate side effect (double-charged customer).
- **No event versioning strategy.** Schema change breaks consumers; plan additive evolution from day one.
- **Synchronous chains across services.** A → B → C → D synchronous event 'cascade' is a distributed monolith; let each service react asynchronously.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Domain event = past-tense business fact**; immutable; describes what happened.
- **Aggregate raises events** on its internal list; doesn't publish.
- **Application layer drains and publishes after commit.**
- **Use records** with IDs + key value objects; never include entire aggregates.
- **In-process:** Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` + `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`.
- **Cross-service:** transactional outbox (or Debezium CDC) to avoid the dual-write problem.
- **Consumers must be idempotent** — at-least-once delivery is the norm.
- **Event names matter** — they're the public language of your system.
- **Plan event versioning** (additive changes only).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What a domain event is**

A fact: something happened that the business cares about. Past tense. Immutable once raised. Describes what occurred, not what should happen.

Good: OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured, EmailVerified, InventoryReserved, RefundIssued.
Bad: PlaceOrder (command), CustomerUpdated (CRUD diff), RowChanged (technical).

Good events make the system expressive, integratable, auditable. Multiple subscribers react without producer knowing. Event log becomes audit log for free. Eventual consistency between aggregates and services is natural.

**Raising events in the aggregate**

Order root has internal events list. create() adds OrderPlacedEvent. cancel() adds OrderCancelledEvent. drainEvents() returns and clears.

Aggregate just records events; doesn't publish. Application layer drains and publishes after persistence. Decoupling lets aggregates stay framework-free and unit-testable.

**Defining events**

Records. Immutable, value equality, succinct. OrderPlacedEvent(orderId, customerId, total, occurredAt) implements DomainEvent.

Guidelines: past tense in name, carry only what subscribers need (IDs + key value objects + timestamp), avoid carrying entire aggregates — events are facts not snapshots.

**Publishing after commit**

Wrong: publish inside transaction. Consumer might query for order before transaction commits — doesn't find it. Or transaction rolls back, you've published phantom event.

Right: publish after commit. Either explicitly drain + publish after the @Transactional method returns, or use Spring's @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) so listeners only fire when transaction has committed.

**In-process vs cross-service**

In-process: ApplicationEventPublisher enough. @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT). Synchronous default or @Async. Listener exceptions don't roll back producer's transaction. Good for same-bounded-context reactions.

Cross-service: publish to Kafka / RabbitMQ. Hit the dual-write problem — what if DB save succeeds but Kafka publish fails or vice versa? Inconsistent state.

**Transactional outbox — reliable cross-service**

In one transaction: save aggregate + insert event rows into outbox table.

Separate worker polls outbox, publishes to Kafka, marks rows as published. Kafka down? Worker retries. Outbox guarantees no event lost.

Schema: outbox(id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, occurred_at, published_at).

Modern alternatives: Debezium CDC streams outbox table directly to Kafka — no separate worker. Kafka transactions also work but outbox simpler and more portable.

**Idempotent consumers — at-least-once reality**

Kafka and most brokers guarantee at-least-once. Your consumer will see same event twice eventually.

Make consumers idempotent: dedupe by event ID (processedEventRepo.existsById), or design side effect harmless on duplicate (UPSERT keyed on aggregate ID, use event ID as natural key for new entities).

Never assume exactly-once without specific broker + consumer guarantees.

**Common mistakes**

- Commands disguised as events — PlaceOrder isn't a fact
- CRUD events — CustomerUpdated says what changed but not why
- Publishing inside transaction — stale data, phantom events
- Entire aggregates in events — bloat, coupling, serialization overhead
- Dual writes — inevitable inconsistency
- Non-idempotent consumers — duplicate side effects (double-charge)
- No event versioning strategy — schema change breaks consumers
- Synchronous chains across services — distributed monolith

**Recommendation**

**Model domain events as past-tense business facts (OrderPlaced, not PlaceOrder); raise them inside aggregate methods on an internal list and drain after persistence. Use Spring's @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) for in-process listeners; for cross-service publication, use the transactional outbox pattern (or Debezium CDC) to avoid the dual-write problem. Make all consumers idempotent because at-least-once delivery is the realistic guarantee. Use records as event types; carry only IDs and key value objects; plan additive schema evolution from day one. Events are your system's public language — name them with care.**

questions.question: How does the Repository pattern work in Domain-Driven Design?
questions.title: Repository Pattern in DDD
questions.direct_answer: A **DDD Repository** is a **collection-like abstraction** for retrieving and persisting **aggregates** (not arbitrary entities or DB rows). It exposes the operations the domain needs in the **domain's language** (`findActiveByCustomerId`, `save(order)`) and **returns whole aggregates**. **One repository per aggregate**, owned by the domain layer, implemented in the persistence adapter (which can use Spring Data JPA, JDBC, MongoDB, or in-memory under the hood). The repository persists the aggregate **atomically** — root and all internal entities together — and is the **only** way external code touches storage for that aggregate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Repository as a domain abstraction (not an infrastructure interface), aggregate-per-repository, why it's not just `JpaRepository`, and how it preserves the consistency boundary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: One repository per JPA entity, returning JPA entities upward, generic CRUD on every aggregate, or putting business logic in repositories.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss specification pattern for complex queries, CQRS-style query services for read paths, and the relationship between aggregate and repository boundary.

sections.title: What a DDD Repository Is (and Isn't)
sections.content:
A repository in DDD is a **collection-like abstraction over aggregates**:

- You ask it for an aggregate by ID, by some domain criteria.
- You hand it an aggregate to save.
- Internally it knows how to translate between the aggregate's shape and storage; externally it speaks the domain's language.

It **is not**:
- A wrapper for every table.
- A generic CRUD interface (`findAll()` over millions of rows).
- A query API for arbitrary projections (use a query service for that).
- A place for business logic.

It **is**:
- One repository per aggregate.
- Returning whole aggregates (root + internals).
- Owned by the domain layer (interface), implemented by the adapter (class).
- The single point of access to storage for that aggregate.

sections.title: Anatomy
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR UC[Use Case] --> Repo[OrderRepository
port - domain layer] Repo -.implemented by.-> Adapter[JpaOrderRepository
adapter layer] Adapter --> SpringData[OrderSpringRepo
JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, String>] SpringData --> DB[(Postgres)] ``` - **Port** lives in the domain (or application) layer; defined in domain language. - **Adapter** lives in the persistence package; uses Spring Data, JDBC, MongoDB, or anything else. - Use case depends on the **port**, never the adapter.

sections.title: Code — Port + Adapter
One Repository Per Aggregate, Not Per Table
sections.content:
**Anti-pattern** — repository per JPA entity:
```java
OrderRepository, OrderItemRepository, ShippingInfoRepository, PaymentMethodRepository
```
The use case must orchestrate four saves to persist one logical change. The aggregate boundary leaks. Transactions become brittle.

**Right shape** — one repository per aggregate:
```java
OrderRepository
```
It persists `Order` *with* its items, shipping info, and payment method together. The persistence adapter handles the multi-table mapping internally. The use case sees one logical `save(order)`.

**The aggregate boundary equals the repository boundary.** A new repository implies a new aggregate. If you find yourself wanting `OrderItemRepository` to update an item in isolation, you're either fragmenting an aggregate that should stay whole, or `OrderItem` should be its own aggregate (rare).

sections.title: Complex Queries — When Repositories Aren't Enough
What Belongs in the Repository (and What Doesn't)
sections.content:
**Belongs:**
- Find / save / delete operations for the aggregate.
- Domain-meaningful finders (`findActiveByCustomerId`, `findOverdueByDueDate`).
- Optimistic-lock handling (translating `OptimisticLockException` to a domain exception if you don't want to leak Spring exceptions).

**Doesn't belong:**
- Business logic (`shouldRefund(order)` — that's a domain service).
- Cross-aggregate coordination (call from the use case, not from the repository).
- Sending emails, publishing events, calling external APIs.
- Caching policy (push to a cache adapter that wraps the repo, not into the repo itself).
- Generic `findAll()` returning unbounded result sets.

**Repository persists; doesn't decide.** Decisions live in the entity (invariants), the use case (orchestration), or domain services (multi-aggregate logic).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Use case importing `JpaRepository`.** JPA leaks upward; framework independence lost.
- **One repository per JPA entity** instead of per aggregate.
- **Returning JPA entities** from the repository port; use case is now coupled to JPA lifecycle.
- **Generic `findAll()`** returning millions of rows. Repositories should expose use-case-driven finders, not raw CRUD.
- **Business logic in repositories** — `OrderRepository.cancelExpired()` instead of an explicit use case.
- **`Specification` API leaking into use cases** — use case asks the port; adapter handles query construction.
- **Mixing read and write models in the repository** — separate query services for read-heavy paths.
- **Inconsistent transaction semantics** — repository methods that silently start their own transaction surprise the use case.

sections.content:
- **Repository = collection-like abstraction over aggregates.**
- **One repository per aggregate**, not per JPA entity.
- **Port in the domain layer; adapter in persistence.**
- **Returns whole aggregates** (root + internal entities), not JPA entities.
- **Domain-meaningful finders** in the domain's language.
- **Specification pattern** for moderately complex queries that still return aggregates.
- **CQRS-style query services** for read-heavy paths returning DTOs.
- **Repository persists; doesn't decide** — no business logic.
- **Aggregate boundary = repository boundary.**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What a DDD repository is**

Collection-like abstraction over aggregates. Ask it for an aggregate by ID or domain criteria; hand it an aggregate to save. Internally translates between aggregate's shape and storage; externally speaks domain language.

Is not: wrapper for every table, generic CRUD interface, query API for arbitrary projections, place for business logic.

Is: one per aggregate, returns whole aggregates (root + internals), owned by domain layer (interface), implemented by adapter (class), single point of access to storage for that aggregate.

**Anatomy**

Port lives in domain (or application) layer; defined in domain language. Adapter lives in persistence package; uses Spring Data, JDBC, MongoDB, anything. Use case depends on port, never adapter.

**Port + adapter code**

Domain: OrderRepository interface with save(Order), findById(OrderId), findByIdempotencyKey(String), findActiveByCustomerId(CustomerId).

Adapter: OrderJpaEntity with @Entity, @Version, @Embedded MoneyEmbeddable, @ElementCollection items. OrderSpringRepo extends JpaRepository with JPA-specific finders. JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository, uses OrderMapper to convert.

Use cases see only OrderRepository. JPA invisible above the adapter.

**One repository per aggregate, not per table**

Anti-pattern: OrderRepository + OrderItemRepository + ShippingInfoRepository + PaymentMethodRepository. Use case orchestrates four saves for one logical change. Aggregate boundary leaks.

Right: just OrderRepository. Persists Order with its items, shipping info, payment method together. Persistence adapter handles multi-table mapping internally.

Aggregate boundary equals repository boundary. New repository implies new aggregate. If you want OrderItemRepository to update an item in isolation, you're fragmenting an aggregate that should stay whole.

**Complex queries**

Repositories awkward for: reporting/analytics, complex search, projection DTOs for UI screens that don't match aggregate shape.

Two patterns:

1. Specification pattern — build composable query criteria, hand to repository. repo.findAll(activeOrdersFor(customerId).and(placedSince(...))). Useful for moderately complex queries still returning aggregates.

2. CQRS-style query services — separate interface returning DTOs. OrderQueryService.findSummary(orderId), search(criteria, page), monthlyStats(month). Returns DTOs not aggregates. Implementation can use SQL views, JPA projections, separate read model. Keeps OrderRepository focused on aggregate lifecycle.

For read-heavy systems, separating commands from queries is the practical move.

**What belongs in the repository**

Belongs: find/save/delete for the aggregate, domain-meaningful finders, optimistic-lock translation to domain exceptions.

Doesn't belong: business logic (that's domain service), cross-aggregate coordination (use case's job), sending emails/publishing events/calling external APIs, caching policy (push to a cache adapter that wraps the repo), generic findAll returning unbounded result sets.

Repository persists; doesn't decide. Decisions in entity (invariants), use case (orchestration), or domain services (multi-aggregate logic).

**Common mistakes**

- Use case importing JpaRepository — framework independence lost
- One repository per JPA entity instead of per aggregate
- Returning JPA entities — use case coupled to JPA lifecycle
- Generic findAll returning millions of rows
- Business logic in repositories — cancelExpired() instead of an explicit use case
- Specification API leaking into use cases — adapter handles query construction
- Mixing read and write models — separate query services for read paths
- Inconsistent transaction semantics — silent transactions surprise the use case

**Recommendation**

**Define one repository per aggregate as a port in the domain layer, written in domain language, returning whole aggregates. Implement in the persistence adapter using Spring Data JPA (or whatever) as the underlying tool — wrap, don't expose. For read-heavy queries that don't match the aggregate shape, add separate CQRS-style query services returning DTOs. Repository persists; doesn't decide — keep business logic in entities, use cases, and domain services. The aggregate boundary equals the repository boundary; if you want a new repository, ask whether you actually need a new aggregate.**

sections.title: Two Different 'Services'
sections.content:
DDD uses 'service' for two very different things — a frequent source of confusion.

**Domain Service:**
- Lives in the domain layer.
- Holds domain logic that doesn't fit on any single entity or value object.
- Typically operates across multiple aggregates.
- Stateless; pure domain code; no Spring, no JPA, no HTTP.
- Named in the domain's language (`PricingPolicy`, `FundsTransferService`, `RouteCalculator`).

**Application Service (= Use Case / Interactor):**
- Lives in the application layer.
- Orchestrates one user goal end-to-end.
- Loads aggregates from repositories, invokes domain logic, saves, publishes events.
- Owns the transaction boundary.
- Knows about infrastructure concerns (transactions, events) but not their implementation.
- Named after the goal (`PlaceOrderUseCase`, `CancelSubscriptionUseCase`).

**Rule of thumb:** if it knows about repositories or transactions, it's an application service. If it just operates on domain objects, it's a domain service — or it should be on an entity.

sections.title: When to Use a Domain Service
sections.content:
**Test 1: 'Could this method live on an entity?'**
- If yes → put it on the entity. Don't create a service.
- `order.cancel()` belongs on `Order`, not in `OrderCancellationService`.

**Test 2: 'Does it operate across multiple aggregates?'**
- If yes → it's a candidate for a domain service.
- `transfer(fromAccount, toAccount, amount)` touches two `Account` aggregates; doesn't belong on either alone.

**Test 3: 'Is it a domain rule or policy with no natural home?'**
- E.g., a `TaxCalculator` that needs jurisdiction lookups, or a `PricingPolicy` that varies by customer tier and time of year.
- These are domain logic but not bound to a specific entity.

**If none of the above, you don't need a domain service.** Most logic should live on entities or value objects.

Owns transaction boundary. Knows about infrastructure concerns but not their implementation. Named after the goal — PlaceOrderUseCase, CancelSubscriptionUseCase.

Rule of thumb: if it knows about repositories or transactions, it's an application service. If it just operates on domain objects, it's a domain service — or it should be on an entity.

**When to use a domain service**

Test 1: could this method live on an entity? If yes, put it on the entity. order.cancel() belongs on Order, not OrderCancellationService.

Test 2: does it operate across multiple aggregates? Yes → candidate for domain service. transfer(fromAccount, toAccount, amount) touches two Account aggregates.

Test 3: domain rule/policy with no natural home? TaxCalculator with jurisdiction lookups, PricingPolicy varying by tier and season. Domain logic but not bound to a specific entity.

If none of the above, you don't need a domain service. Most logic on entities or value objects.

**Domain service example**

FundsTransferService.transfer(from, to, amount) checks from.canDebit(amount), calls from.debit(amount), to.credit(amount). No @Service, no Spring, no @Transactional, no repository calls. Operates on already-loaded aggregates.

Application service is what loads/saves: TransferFundsUseCase pulls Account aggregates from repository, calls transferService.transfer(from, to, amount), saves both. @Transactional on use case.

Clean split: use case handles I/O and transactions; domain service handles the domain rule.

**Application service — thin orchestration**

Application services are thin. Their job is plumbing:

1. Pull aggregates via repositories
2. Delegate to entities / value objects / domain services
3. Persist the result
4. Publish domain events
5. Manage transaction boundary

PlaceOrderUseCase.execute(cmd): construct Order, reserve inventory, order.submit(), orderRepo.save(order), events.publishAll(order.drainEvents()), return order.id().

No business logic in this method. Every business decision (cancel, submit, addItem) lives in Order or a domain service. The use case is a script: load, decide via domain, save, emit.

**The anti-pattern: logic in application services**

Developers default to Spring @Service and pour business logic in. OrderService.cancel(id) loads order, checks if SHIPPED, sets CANCELLED, saves. Now business rule duplicated in every cancel flow (refund, admin, scheduled). Order is anemic; invalid state reachable via setStatus from anywhere. Fat service classes accumulate dozens of methods.

Fix: push rule into entity. Order.cancel() checks status, mutates, raises event. CancelOrderUseCase loads, calls o.cancel(), saves, publishes events.

**Common mistakes**

- Calling everything 'a service' — OrderService doing cancellation rules + HTTP→DB mixes layers
- Domain services for everything — most logic belongs on entities
- Application services with business logic — anemic entities + fat services = classic anti-pattern
- Domain services with @Transactional or repositories — they should know about domain objects only
- One huge OrderService — split by use case
- Domain service that's actually a calculator — fine as static method on value object
- Confusing 'domain service' with Spring @Service — stereotype doesn't tell you which kind

**Recommendation**

**Default to putting logic on entities and value objects. Reach for a domain service only when the logic genuinely spans multiple aggregates or has no natural home. Application services (use cases) are thin orchestrators — one per user goal — that load aggregates, delegate to domain logic, save, and publish events. Application services contain no business rules; domain services contain no infrastructure concerns. Spring's @Service annotation tells you nothing about layer; the package and dependencies do.**

questions.question: What is the Ubiquitous Language in DDD and how do you establish it on a team?
questions.title: Ubiquitous Language in DDD
questions.direct_answer: The **Ubiquitous Language** is a **shared vocabulary** — used by developers, domain experts, product, and the code itself — in which **every business term has one precise meaning**. It eliminates translation between conversation and code: when the domain expert says 'qualify a lead', the code says `lead.qualify(criteria)`. You establish it through **collaborative modeling** (Event Storming, glossaries, code reviews), enforce it in **code (class, method, event names)**, and **scope it to one Bounded Context** (the same word can mean different things in different BCs). It's the most important practice in DDD — and the cheapest to start with.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating it as 'just naming conventions', or trying to make one language span the entire enterprise.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Event Storming as a discovery tool, code-review culture for language enforcement, and the link between Ubiquitous Language and bounded contexts.

sections.title: The Translation Cost Problem
sections.content:
Without an Ubiquitous Language, every conversation between business and engineering pays a **translation tax**:

- Domain expert: 'When the lead qualifies, we hand it to the rep.'
- Developer hears: 'Update `prospect.status = QUALIFIED` and assign `salesPersonId`.'
- Code: `prospectService.updateStatus(prospect, 'qualified'); prospect.salesPersonId = repId;`

Three different vocabularies. Every code review, every requirements discussion, every bug report requires translation. Misunderstandings creep in silently:

- Developer doesn't realize that 'qualified' has nuanced criteria.
- Domain expert doesn't realize that the code path doesn't validate those criteria.
- The bug is found three months later in production.

**Ubiquitous Language eliminates this tax.** The conversation, the documents, the code, the database column names, the event names — all use the same words. When the domain expert says 'qualify', the code says `qualify`. When the code does something the words don't describe, **the words evolve** — not a parallel translation.

sections.title: Language Lives in the Code
Discovery — Event Storming and Conversations
sections.content:
Ubiquitous Language isn't designed in advance — it's **discovered** by talking to domain experts.

**Event Storming (Alberto Brandolini)** is the canonical technique:

1. Gather domain experts + developers in a room (or virtual whiteboard).
2. Sticky-note all the business events that happen, in past tense (`OrderPlaced`, `LeadQualified`, `PaymentCaptured`).
3. Cluster related events; identify the commands that trigger them, the actors who issue them, the policies / rules.
4. Names of events / commands / aggregates that emerge are the seeds of the Ubiquitous Language.

**Lighter-weight techniques:**
- **Glossary** maintained alongside code; reviewed periodically.
- **Domain expert in code reviews** — catches naming drift.
- **Storytelling sessions** where a domain expert walks through a real customer journey using their own words; engineers note vocabulary.
- **Refactor-as-you-learn** — when a new term emerges, rename in code immediately. IDEs make this safe.

sections.title: Ubiquitous Language Is Per Bounded Context
sections.content:
**Ubiquitous Language is bounded.** The same word can have different meanings in different Bounded Contexts — and that's correct.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sales[Sales BC]
        SC[Customer = prospect with lead score]
    end
    subgraph Shipping[Shipping BC]
        SHC[Customer = delivery address with prefs]
    end
    subgraph Support[Support BC]
        SUC[Customer = ticket holder with SLA]
    end
```

Forcing one global meaning across all contexts produces:
- A `Customer` god-class with conflicting concerns.
- Coupling between teams.
- A vocabulary nobody fully agrees on.

**Per-context language** lets each context have a clean, internally consistent vocabulary. When data crosses a boundary, **translate explicitly** (Anti-Corruption Layer or domain events with primitive payloads).

sections.title: Establishing It On a Real Team — Practical Steps
sections.content:
1. **Run an Event Storming session** with domain experts and engineers. 2-3 hours; come away with sticky notes you can photograph and translate into a glossary.
2. **Start a glossary** — a `GLOSSARY.md` in the repo. Each term: definition, example, synonyms to avoid. Keep it short (50 terms, not 500).
3. **Rename in code** — IDE refactor across the package. The first big rename is the hardest; subsequent ones are cheap.
4. **Adopt naming conventions for events / commands / aggregates** — events past tense, commands imperative, queries nounal.
5. **Code review for language** — reviewers flag class/method names that don't match the glossary or that introduce new terms.
6. **Domain experts in design discussions** — they catch language drift before it solidifies in code.
7. **Document only at the boundary** — OpenAPI, event schemas, public interface docs. Internal class names *are* the documentation.
8. **Refactor when language evolves** — new term in the business? Rename in code immediately. Don't let parallel vocabularies coexist.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Just a glossary'** — a wiki that nobody updates. The language must live in the code.
- **One global language** — forcing all contexts to share vocabulary recreates the unified-model trap.
- **Translating in code reviews** — 'this PR uses `Prospect`, but our docs say `Lead`' caught only sometimes — silently drifts.
- **Tech-flavored names** — `OrderManager`, `OrderHandler`, `OrderProcessor`, `OrderHelper` — mean nothing to domain experts.
- **Synonyms used loosely** — `User`, `Customer`, `Account`, `Client` interchangeably. Pick one per context; ban the others.
- **Renaming reluctance** — 'we'll fix the naming later.' Later is never. Rename now while the code is small.
- **Ignoring domain experts.** Engineers inventing names is how 'OrderHandlerService' is born.

sections.content:

- **Eliminates translation tax** between conversation and implementation.
- **Per Bounded Context** — the same word can mean different things in different BCs.
- **Discovered through Event Storming** and continuous conversation with domain experts.
- **Enforced by code review and refactoring**, not by wishful thinking.
- **Tests reinforce the language** — readable test names *are* documentation.
- **The cheapest, highest-leverage DDD practice** — doable on day one of a project.

questions.question: What is the Anti-Corruption Layer pattern in DDD and when do you use it?
questions.title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) Pattern in DDD
questions.direct_answer: An **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)** is a **translation layer** placed between your bounded context and an external system (legacy, third-party, or another team's BC) to **prevent the foreign model from leaking into yours**. It exposes a clean interface in *your* domain language, hides the foreign system's quirks (different vocabulary, different semantics, mismatched data shapes), and is the **only** place that knows the foreign model. Use it whenever you integrate with a system you don't control — a legacy ERP, a third-party CRM, or a team that uses different terminology. Without an ACL, the foreign model corrupts yours.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Skipping the ACL because 'it's just a wrapper'; the foreign model leaks via 'temporary' direct usage that becomes permanent.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss ACL as a Hexagonal driven adapter, the cost of building one, and when *not* to (e.g., trusted internal partner with shared kernel).

sections.title: The Corruption Problem
sections.content:
When you integrate with an external system, you face two unappetizing options:

**Option 1: Adopt their model.** Use their classes, their vocabulary, their data shapes throughout your code.
- Their Customer has 47 fields you don't need.
- Their `customer_type` enum has values like `NA-OLD-3` that mean nothing in your domain.
- Their concept of 'order status' overlaps yours but with different lifecycle states.
- Schema changes they make break your code.
- Your codebase now reads in their language, not yours.

**Option 2: Build an Anti-Corruption Layer.** Translate at the boundary; keep your domain pure.
- A small adapter is the **only** place that imports their classes.
- It exposes operations in *your* domain language: `submitOrder(Order)`, not `executeTransaction(LegacyTxn)`.
- It translates fields, statuses, semantics.
- When they change, you change the ACL — not the rest of your code.

**Option 1 always loses long-term.** The foreign model corrupts yours; future migrations and refactors become risky. The ACL is the price of integrating with systems you don't control.

- Integrating with a **third-party API** (Stripe, Salesforce, SAP) whose model is shaped by their concerns, not yours.
- Integrating with **another team's Bounded Context** when their model differs significantly from yours.
- Strangler-fig migration: the new system uses an ACL to talk to the legacy system during the transition.
- The foreign model is **unstable** — frequent breaking changes; you want one place to absorb them.

**Skip ACL when:**
- The two contexts share a **Shared Kernel** — a small, stable, agreed-upon vocabulary (only safe with trusted internal partners).
- The integration is **trivial** and read-only (a one-way data dump where you just store their JSON).
- Both teams agree on a **Published Language** (Avro/Protobuf schema) and the model is close enough that translation is mechanical.

Even in 'skip' cases, ask: 'when their model changes, who pays?' If you do, you want at least a thin translator in case it grows.

sections.title: ACL in Strangler-Fig Migrations
sections.content:
An ACL is the centerpiece of safely migrating off a legacy monolith. ```mermaid flowchart LR Client([Client]) --> Facade[Facade] Facade -->|new flows| NewSvc[New Service
clean domain model] Facade -->|old flows| Legacy[Legacy Monolith
old model] NewSvc -->|when needs legacy data| ACL[ACL adapter] ACL --> Legacy ``` During migration: - The new service uses its own clean domain model. - When it needs data the legacy still owns (customers, orders, products), it goes through the ACL. - The ACL translates the legacy's quirks into the new domain's vocabulary. - As ownership of data moves to the new service, the ACL shrinks; eventually it disappears when the legacy is decommissioned. Without the ACL, the new service inherits all the legacy's vocabulary and ages prematurely.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Just for now'** — importing the legacy model directly because the ACL is 'too much code'. The temporary becomes permanent; the legacy model spreads.
- **Translation logic in use cases.** A use case that looks up `legacyCustomer.getTierCd()` and maps to your tier inline — the ACL has been bypassed.
- **Returning the legacy model from the ACL.** ACL must return your domain types only; otherwise it's a thin wrapper, not a translation layer.
- **No tests on the translator.** Translators are where bugs live (legacy enum changes break your domain silently). Test them with real legacy fixtures.
- **One ACL for many foreign systems.** Each foreign system deserves its own ACL with its own translator.
- **ACL bloat.** ACL grows business logic over time. Keep it pure translation; push business decisions back into your domain.

sections.content:

- **Protects your domain model** from foreign vocabulary, semantics, and instability.
- **Adapter + translator** structure; adapter implements a port in your language.
- **Foreign model imports contained** inside the ACL package only.
- **Use for** legacy integrations, third-party APIs, other teams' BCs with different models, strangler-fig migrations.
- **Skip for** trusted shared-kernel partners or trivial integrations.
- **The translator is where bugs live** — test thoroughly with real fixtures.
- **Without an ACL, the foreign model corrupts yours** — the integration debt compounds.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The corruption problem**

When integrating with an external system, two options:

Option 1: adopt their model. Their Customer has 47 fields you don't need, their customer_type enum is NA-OLD-3, their order status overlaps yours with different lifecycle states. Schema changes break your code. Your codebase reads in their language.

Option 2: build an Anti-Corruption Layer. Translate at the boundary; keep your domain pure. Small adapter is the only place that imports their classes. Exposes operations in your language. Translates fields, statuses, semantics. When they change, you change the ACL — not the rest of your code.

Option 1 always loses long-term. ACL is the price of integrating with systems you don't control.

**Architecture**

Port (CrmGateway) in your domain layer, speaks your language. Adapter implements the port; lives in ACL. Translator classes do field-level conversion. Foreign model imported only inside the ACL package.

**Code example**

Domain: CrmGateway interface with findCustomer(CustomerId), recordContact(CustomerId, ContactType). Customer record with id, name, email, tier.

ACL adapter: LegacyCrmGatewayAdapter implements CrmGateway. Uses LegacyCrmClient + LegacyCustomerTranslator. findCustomer fetches LegacyCustomer, maps via translator. recordContact maps your ContactType enum to legacy 'PH-1', 'EM-NEW', 'IP-V2' codes.

Translator: maps LegacyCustomer (custIdent, firstNm, lastNm, emlAddr1, tierCd) to domain Customer. Maps tier code 'T1-OLD'/'T1-NEW' → GOLD, 'T2' → SILVER, default → BRONZE.

Use cases see CrmGateway + Customer — your language. Legacy CRM types contained inside ACL.

**When to use**

- Integrating with legacy system with different model/vocabulary
- Integrating with third-party API (Stripe, Salesforce, SAP) shaped by their concerns
- Integrating with another team's BC with different model
- Strangler-fig migration during transition
- Foreign model unstable — frequent breaking changes

**When to skip**

- Two contexts share a Shared Kernel (small, stable, agreed-upon vocabulary; only with trusted internal partners)
- Integration is trivial and read-only
- Both teams agree on a Published Language (Avro/Protobuf) and model is close enough

Even in skip cases ask: when their model changes, who pays? If you do, want at least a thin translator.

**ACL in strangler-fig migrations**

New service uses its own clean domain model. When it needs data the legacy owns (customers, orders, products), goes through the ACL. ACL translates legacy quirks into new domain's vocabulary.

As ownership moves to new service, ACL shrinks; eventually disappears when legacy decommissioned.

Without ACL, new service inherits all legacy vocabulary and ages prematurely.

**Common mistakes**

- 'Just for now' — importing legacy model directly; temporary becomes permanent
- Translation logic in use cases — use case looks up legacyCustomer.getTierCd() and maps inline; ACL bypassed
- Returning legacy model from ACL — must return your domain types only
- No tests on the translator — where bugs live; legacy enum changes break domain silently
- One ACL for many foreign systems — each deserves its own with its own translator
- ACL bloat — grows business logic over time; keep it pure translation

**Recommendation**

**Always build an Anti-Corruption Layer when integrating with a system you don't control — legacy, third-party, or another team's BC with different vocabulary. Place a clean port in your domain language, implement it in an adapter, hide the translator behind it. Foreign model imports stay contained inside the ACL package. Test the translator thoroughly with real fixtures — it's where breakage lurks. Skip the ACL only when you have a stable shared kernel with a trusted partner or a trivial read-only integration. The cost of writing an ACL is far less than the cost of a foreign model spreading through your codebase.**

questions.question: How do you implement DDD tactical patterns in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: DDD Tactical Patterns in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: In Spring Boot, implement DDD tactical patterns by **packaging per Bounded Context**, keeping the **domain layer free of Spring/JPA annotations**, putting **invariants on entities and value objects**, defining **repositories as ports** in the domain, and writing **use cases as plain classes wired by `@Configuration`**. Use **records for value objects**, **`@Version` on aggregate roots** for optimistic concurrency, **`@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`** for in-process domain events, and the **transactional outbox** for cross-service events. Keep JPA entities as adapter-layer mapping artifacts — separate from domain entities. Spring lives in adapters and configuration, never in the domain.

sections.content:
- **`@Entity` on the domain entity.** Couples the domain to JPA — lazy proxies, dirty checking, lifecycle hooks. Keep domain entity and JPA entity separate.
- **`@Service` on the aggregate or value object.** They're not Spring beans.
- **`JpaRepository` as the domain repository.** Wrap it in an adapter implementing a domain port.
- **`@Transactional` on the controller.** Wrong layer; use case is the right boundary.
- **No optimistic lock.** `@Version` is essentially free and prevents last-write-wins corruption.
- **Cross-bounded-context imports.** Sales pulling `Shipping.Order` directly. Use ArchUnit / Spring Modulith.
- **Publishing events inside the transaction.** Use `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` for in-process; outbox for cross-service.

sections.content:
- **Package per Bounded Context** (`com.example.sales/domain|application|adapter|config`).

- **Use cases (application services) plain;** `@Transactional` on the implementation; wired by `@Configuration`.
- **Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` + `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`** for in-process events.
- **Transactional outbox + Debezium / Kafka** for cross-service events.
- **Enforce boundaries** with ArchUnit / Spring Modulith / Java modules.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Project structure per BC**

Package per Bounded Context: com.example.sales.{domain,application,adapter,config}. domain = entities, value objects, domain services, events. application = use cases, ports. adapter = web (controllers), persistence (JPA + mappers), external clients. config = @Configuration wiring.

Multiple BCs as sibling packages — sales, shipping, support.

Boundary enforcement: ArchUnit rules in CI prevent sales from importing shipping.domain.*. Spring Modulith provides this out of the box.

**Value objects with records**

Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) record. Compact constructor validates non-null + decimal places. plus(), zero() methods on the type. No Spring, no JPA. Records give immutability + equals/hashCode/toString for free.

OrderId(String value) record. next() generates UUID. Strongly typed IDs prevent passing CustomerId where OrderId expected.

**Aggregate root with invariants and events**

Order class. OrderId, CustomerId, items, status, total, internal events list. Constructor validates 'order needs items'. create() factory raises OrderPlacedEvent. cancel() validates status, mutates, raises OrderCancelledEvent. drainEvents() returns + clears.

Zero Spring imports, zero JPA. Pure domain code, unit-testable in milliseconds.

**Repository port + JPA adapter**

Domain layer: OrderRepository interface with save(Order), findById(OrderId).

Adapter layer: OrderJpaEntity (@Entity, @Version, @Embedded MoneyEmbeddable, @ElementCollection items). MoneyEmbeddable. OrderSpringRepo extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, String>. JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository, uses OrderMapper to convert domain Order ↔ OrderJpaEntity.

Domain Order and OrderJpaEntity are separate types. @Version on JPA entity gives optimistic locking at aggregate-root level. Use case sees only OrderRepository.

**Application service + transactions**

PlaceOrderUseCase interface. PlaceOrderCommand record.

PlaceOrderInteractor implements it. Constructor injection of OrderRepository, InventoryGateway, ApplicationEventPublisher. @Transactional on execute(): reserve inventory, create Order, save, drainEvents and publish.

@Configuration wires it via @Bean. @Transactional on use case implementation — natural transaction boundary.

**Domain events with Spring**

@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) for in-process listeners. Ensures listener runs only after producer's transaction committed — no phantom events on rollback, no stale reads.

For cross-service: transactional outbox. In same transaction, save aggregate + insert event rows into outbox table. Separate worker (or Debezium CDC) publishes from outbox to Kafka.

Outbox schema: id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload (JSONB), occurred_at, published_at.

**Domain service in Spring**

FundsTransferService is plain Java — transfer(from, to, amount) checks canDebit, calls debit + credit. Wired by @Configuration as @Bean. Use case loads accounts, hands to domain service, saves.

**Common mistakes**

- @Entity on domain entity — couples to JPA lazy proxies, dirty checking, lifecycle hooks
- @Service on aggregate or value object — they're not beans
- JpaRepository as domain repository — wrap in adapter implementing domain port
- @Transactional on controller — wrong layer
- No optimistic lock — @Version is free; prevents last-write-wins corruption
- Cross-BC imports — use ArchUnit / Spring Modulith
- Publishing events inside the transaction — use AFTER_COMMIT or outbox
- Skipping mapper — same class as domain entity AND @Entity annotated 'to save time'; short-term win, long-term coupling

**Recommendation**

**Implement DDD tactical patterns in Spring Boot by keeping the domain layer pure Java — records for value objects, plain classes for aggregates, no framework annotations. Map domain entities to separate JPA entities in the persistence adapter. Define repositories as ports owned by the domain; implement them with Spring Data wrapped in an adapter. Put @Transactional on use case implementations, use @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) for in-process events, and the transactional outbox for cross-service. Enforce per-BC boundaries with ArchUnit or Spring Modulith. Spring lives in adapters and configuration, never in the domain.**
